'''''Aesculus hippocastanum''''', the '''horse chestnut''',{{r|IUCN|usda|vascan}} is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the [[maple]], [[Sapindus|soapberry]] and [[lychee]] family [[Sapindaceae]]. It is a large, [[deciduous]], [[synoecious]] (hermaphroditic-flowered) tree.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://bioweb.uwlax.edu/bio203/s2013/phillips_reb2/reproduction.htm| website= bioweb.uwlax.edu| publisher= [[University of Wisconsin La Crosse]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150130212408/https://bioweb.uwlax.edu/bio203/s2013/phillips_reb2/reproduction.htm |title=''Aesculus hippocastanum'': Reproduction |archive-date=2015-01-30}}</ref> It is also called '''horse-chestnut''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> '''European horsechestnut''',{{r|ncsu}} '''buckeye''',{{r|nccih}} and '''conker tree'''.{{r|coles2015}} It is not to be confused with the sweet chestnut or Spanish chestnut, ''[[Castanea sativa]]'', which is a tree in another family, [[Fagaceae]].<ref name=Stace>{{cite book|last=Stace|first=C. A.|author-link=Stace, C. A.|year=2010|title=New Flora of the British Isles|edition=Third|publisher=Cambridge University Press|location=Cambridge, UK|isbn=978-0-521-70772-5}}</ref>{{rp|371}}

==Description==
''Aesculus hippocastanum'' is a large tree, growing to about {{convert|39|m|ft}} tall<ref name=Stace/> with a domed crown of stout branches. On old trees, the outer branches are often pendulous with curled-up tips. The [[leaf|leaves]] are opposite and [[palmate]]ly compound, with 5–7 leaflets {{convert|13|–|30|cm|in|frac=2|abbr=on}} long, making the whole leaf up to {{convert|60|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} across, with a {{convert|7|–|20|cm|in|frac=2|abbr=on}} petiole. The leaf scars left on twigs after the leaves have fallen have a distinctive [[horseshoe]] shape, complete with seven "nails". The [[flower]]s are usually white with a yellow to pink blotch at the base of the petals;<ref name=Stace/> they are produced in spring in erect panicles {{convert|10|–|30|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} tall with about 20–50 flowers on each panicle. Its pollen is not poisonous for honey bees.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://beespoke.info/2014/02/10/bee-trees-horse-chestnut/|title=Bee Trees - Horse Chestnut |website=beespoke.info| publisher= }}</ref> Usually only 1–5 [[fruit]]s develop on each panicle. The shell is a green, spiky [[capsule (fruit)|capsule]] containing one (rarely two or three) [[nut (fruit)|nut]]-like [[seed]]s called conkers or horse-chestnuts. Each conker is {{convert|2|–|4|cm|in|frac=4|abbr=on}} in diameter, glossy nut-brown with a whitish scar at the base.<ref name=rushforth>{{cite book| last= Rushforth| first= K.| year= 1999| title= Trees of Britain and Europe| publisher= Collins | isbn= 0-00-220013-9}}</ref>

==Etymology==
The common name horse chestnut originates from the similarity of the leaves and fruits to sweet chestnuts, ''[[Castanea sativa]]'' (a tree in a different family, the [[Fagaceae]]),<ref name=Stace/> together with the alleged observation that the fruit or seeds could help panting or coughing horses.<ref>{{cite journal |last= Lack| first= H. Walter |title=The Discovery and Rediscovery of the Horse Chestnut |journal= [[Arnoldia (journal)|Arnoldia]]| publisher= Harvard University |volume=61 |issue=4 |url= http://arnoldia.arboretum.harvard.edu/pdf/articles/628.pdf |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100727173454/http://arnoldia.arboretum.harvard.edu/pdf/articles/628.pdf|archive-date=2010-07-27 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last= Little |first=Elbert L. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Trees: Western Region |year=1994 |orig-date=1980 |publisher=Knopf |isbn=0-394-50761-4 |page=541}}</ref>
[[File: Hortus Haren (Groningen) 13-12-2025. (actm.) 05.jpg |thumb|260px|Typical rootstock of a ''Aesculus hippocastanum.'']]

Although it is sometimes known as [[Buckeye (tree)|buckeye]],{{r|nccih}} for the resemblance of the seed to a [[deer]]'s eye, the term ''buckeye'' is more commonly used for [[New World]] members of the genus ''[[Aesculus]]'',{{r|wott2018}} such as ''[[Aesculus glabra]]''.

==Distribution and habitat==
The [[native species|native]] distribution of ''Aesculus hippocastanum'' given by different sources varies. {{As of|2023|March}}, [[Plants of the World Online]] considered it to be native to the [[Balkans]] ([[Albania]], [[Bulgaria]], [[Greece]] and former [[Yugoslavia]]), but also to [[Turkey]] and [[Turkmenistan]].<ref name="POWO_781594-1">{{cite web |title=''Aesculus hippocastanum'' L.. |work=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew|url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:781594-1 |access-date=2023-03-28 }}</ref> A 2017 assessment for the [[IUCN Red List]] restricted the native distribution to the Balkan area: Albania, Bulgaria, mainland Greece and [[North Macedonia]].<ref name=IUCN/> It has been introduced and planted around the world. It can be found in many parts of Europe as far north as [[Harstad Municipality|Harstad]] north of the [[Arctic Circle]] in [[Norway]],<ref>{{cite web | url=https://planteportalen.no/lovtraer/parkhestekastanje/ | title=Hestekastanje | website= planteportalen.no| date= | publisher= }}</ref> and [[Gästrikland]] in [[Sweden]] as well as in many parks and cities around the northern US and Canada such as [[Edmonton]] in [[Alberta]], Canada.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.edmontonmapsheritage.ca/location/holowach-tree/ | title=Holowach Tree | website= edmontonmapsheritage.ca| publisher= | archive-date=2023-09-23 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20230923213158/http://www.edmontonmapsheritage.ca/location/holowach-tree/ | access-date=2023-10-07}}</ref>

The compact native population of horse chestnut in Bulgaria is distinct from the horse chestnut forests of northern Greece, western North Macedonia and Albania. It is limited to an area of {{cvt|9|ha}} in the [[Veliki Preslav|Preslav]] Mountain north of the [[Balkan Mountains]], in the valleys of the Dervishka and Lazarska rivers. Bulgaria's [[relict]] horse chestnut forests are critically endangered at the national level and protected as part of the Dervisha Managed Nature Reserve.<ref name="bas">{{Cite web |title=Forests of Horse chestnut (Aesculus hippocastanum) | work= Red Data Book of Bulgaria |url= http://e-ecodb.bas.bg/rdb/en/vol3/29G1.html |via=e-ecodb.bas.bg |access-date=2023-02-10}}</ref>

== Cultivation and uses ==
It is widely cultivated in streets and parks throughout the [[temperateness|temperate]] world, and has been particularly successful in places like [[Ireland]], Great Britain and New Zealand, where it is commonly found in parks, streets and avenues. Cultivation for its spectacular spring flowers is successful in a wide range of [[temperateness|temperate]] climatic conditions provided summers are not too hot, with trees being grown as far north as [[Edmonton]], Alberta, Canada,<ref>{{cite web| url= http://www.edmonton.ca/city_government/documents/HistoricResourcesInventory.xls |title= Historical Resources Inventory| publisher= City of Edmonton, Alberta| website= edmonton.ca}}</ref> the [[Faroe Islands]],<ref>{{cite journal| last1= Højgaard| first1= A.| last2=  Jóhansen| first2= J.| last3= Ødum| first3= S. |year= 1989| title= A century of [[tree planting]] on the Faroe Islands| journal= Ann. Soc. Sci. Faeroensis| number= Supplementum 14| url= }}</ref> [[Reykjavík]], Iceland and [[Harstad Municipality|Harstad]], Norway.

In Britain and Ireland, the seeds are used for the popular children's game [[conkers]]. During the [[First World War]], there was a campaign to ask for everyone (including children) to collect the seeds and donate them to the government. The conkers were used as a source of starch for fermentation using the ''[[Clostridium acetobutylicum]]'' method devised by [[Chaim Weizmann]] to produce [[acetone]] for use as a solvent for the production of [[cordite]], which was then used in military armaments. Weizmann's process could use any source of starch, but the government chose to ask for conkers to avoid causing starvation by depleting food sources. But conkers were found to be a poor source, and the factory only produced acetone for three months; however, they were collected again in the [[Second World War]] for the same reason.<ref>{{cite web| url= https://www.bbc.co.uk/radio4/history/making_history/makhist10_prog3d.shtml|title=Conkers - collected for use in two world wars|work=Making history| publisher= BBC|access-date=27 September 2014}}</ref>

[[Image:Aesculus hippocastanum fruit.jpg|thumb|A selection of fresh conkers]]

The seeds, especially those that are young and fresh, are slightly poisonous, containing [[alkaloid]] [[saponin]]s and [[glucoside]]s. Although not dangerous to touch, they cause sickness when eaten; consumed by horses, they can cause tremors and lack of coordination.<ref>{{cite book|title=Feeding and care of the horse|first=Lon D.|last=Lewis|publisher=Wiley-Blackwell|year=1995|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=m4VM9__SKJMC&pg=PA303| page= 303| isbn= 978-0-683-04967-1| access-date=2011-10-21}}</ref>

The horse-chestnut is a favorite subject for [[bonsai]].<ref name="Ma-Ke_Aesculus hippocastanum">{{cite web |first=Mark |last=D'Cruz |title=Ma-Ke Bonsai Care Guide for Aesculus hippocastanum |publisher=Ma-Ke Bonsai |url=http://makebonsai.com/guide/bonsailink.asp?quicklink=5082&name=Aesculus_hippocastanum |access-date=2011-07-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120315170441/http://makebonsai.com/guide/bonsailink.asp?quicklink=5082&name=Aesculus_hippocastanum |archive-date=2012-03-15 }}</ref>

Though the seeds are said to repel spiders, there is little evidence to support these claims. The presence of saponin may repel insects, but it is not clear whether this is effective on spiders.<ref name='RSC'>{{cite web |url= http://www.thereaction.net/news/y2010/m10/spiders_versus_conkers_definitive_guide.aspx |title=Spiders vs conkers: the definitive guide |access-date=2013-09-09 |last=Edwards |first=Jon |year=2010 |publisher=[[Royal Society of Chemistry]] |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20130906155709/http://www.thereaction.net/news/y2010/m10/spiders_versus_conkers_definitive_guide.aspx |archive-date=2013-09-06 }}</ref>

''Aesculus hippocastanum'' is affected by the leaf-mining moth ''[[Cameraria ohridella]]'', whose larvae feed on horse chestnut leaves. The moth was described from [[North Macedonia]] where the species was discovered in 1984 but took 18 years to reach Britain.<ref name="Lees et al. 2009">{{cite web| last1= Lees| first1=  D.C.| last2= Lopez-Vaamonde| first2= C.| last3= Augustin| first3= S.| year= 2009| title= Taxon page for Cameraria ohridella | publisher= Deschka & Dimic |url= http://www.eol.org/pages/306084| access-date= 2009-08-10}}</ref>

In Germany, they are commonly planted in [[beer garden]]s, particularly in [[Bavaria]]. Prior to the advent of mechanical refrigeration, brewers would dig cellars for [[lager]]ing. To further protect the cellars from the summer heat, they would plant horse chestnut trees, which have spreading, dense canopies but shallow roots which would not intrude on the caverns. The practice of serving beer at these sites evolved into the modern beer garden.<ref>{{cite news |last=Schäffer |first=Albert |date=2012-05-21 |title=120 Minuten sind nicht genug |trans-title=120 minutes aren't enough |url=https://www.faz.net/aktuell/gesellschaft/biergaerten-120-minuten-sind-nicht-genug-11759037.html |language=de |newspaper=[[Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung]] |access-date=2016-10-11}}</ref>

An inexpensive detergent for washing clothes can be made at home from conkers, and this is said to be an environmentally benign ('eco-friendly') detergent.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.instructables.com/How-to-Make-Laundry-Detergent-From-Conkers-Horse-C/ | title=How to Make Laundry Detergent from Conkers (Horse Chestnuts) | website= instructables.com | publisher= | date= }}</ref>

===Traditional medicine and research===
[[File:Beta-Aescin.svg|thumb|right|[[Aescin]]]]
The seed [[extract]] standardized to around 20 percent [[aescin]] (escin) is possibly useful in [[traditional medicine]] for its effect on [[vein|venous]] tone.<ref>{{cite journal |pmid=8569363|year=1996|last1=Diehm|first1=C.|title=Comparison of leg compression stocking and oral horse-chestnut seed extract therapy in patients with chronic venous insufficiency|journal=Lancet|volume=347|issue=8997|pages=292–4|last2=Trampisch|first2=H. J.| last3=Lange |first3=S.| last4=Schmidt |first4=C.|doi=10.1016/s0140-6736(96)90467-5|s2cid=20408233|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name= nccih>{{cite web |url= https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/horse-chestnut |title=Horse chestnut |website= nccih.nih.gov |publisher=[[National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health]] |date=1 October 2020 |access-date=27 October 2022}}</ref> 

A 2012 [[Cochrane Review]] of low-quality studies suggested that horse chestnut seed extract may be an efficacious and safe short-term treatment for [[chronic venous insufficiency]], but definitive [[randomized controlled trial]]s had not been conducted to confirm the efficacy.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1= Pittler |first1=Max H|last2=Ernst |first2=Edzard |date=2012-11-14 |title=Horse chestnut seed extract for chronic venous insufficiency |journal=The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews |volume=11 |issue=11 |article-number=CD003230 |doi=10.1002/14651858.CD003230.pub4 |issn=1469-493X |pmc=7144685 |pmid= 23152216}}</ref>

===Safety===
There is risk of [[acute kidney injury]], "when patients, who had undergone cardiac surgery were given high doses of horse chestnut extract i.v. for postoperative [[oedema]]. The phenomenon was dose dependent as no alteration in kidney function was recorded with 340 μg/kg, mild kidney function impairment developed with 360 μg/kg and acute kidney injury with 510 μg/kg".<ref>{{cite book |isbn=0-85369-429-X |pages=[https://archive.org/details/martindale00kath/page/1543 1543–4] |title=Martindale: The complete drug reference|last1=Parfitt |first1=Kathleen |year=1999 |publisher=Pharmaceutical Press |url=https://archive.org/details/martindale00kath/page/1543 }}</ref>

Raw horse chestnut seed, leaf, bark and flower are toxic due to the presence of [[aesculin]] and should not be ingested. Horse chestnut seed is classified by the FDA as an unsafe herb.<ref name=mskcc>{{cite web|url=http://wWw.mskcc.org/cancer-care/herb/horse-chestnut|publisher= [[Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center]]|title=Horse chestnut|date=29 March 2022|access-date=27 October 2022}}</ref> The [[glycoside]] and [[saponin]] constituents are considered toxic.<ref name=mskcc/>

==Diseases==
[[File:10 Pest damage - horse-chestnut leaf miner (Cameraria ohridella) in Parma, Italy.jpg|thumb|Horse-chestnut leaf miner (''[[Cameraria ohridella]]'') tree damage in Parma, Italy]]
* [[Bleeding canker of horse chestnut|Bleeding canker]]. Half of all horse-chestnuts in Great Britain are now showing symptoms to some degree of this potentially lethal bacterial infection.<ref>{{cite web|title=Extent of the bleeding canker of horse chestnut problem |url= http://www.forestresearch.gov.uk/website/forestresearch.nsf/ByUnique/INFD-6KYBN2|publisher=UK Forestry Commission|access-date=2010-01-09|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20091209155126/http://www.forestresearch.gov.uk/website/forestresearch.nsf/ByUnique/INFD-6KYBN2
|archive-date= 2009-12-09}}</ref><ref name="suffolkcoastal">{{cite web |url= http://www.suffolkcoastal.gov.uk/yourdistrict/trees/chestnuts/default.htm |title=Horse chestnut pest and disease problems |website= suffolkcoastal.gov.uk |access-date=15 January 2022 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110923153854/http://www.suffolkcoastal.gov.uk/yourdistrict/trees/chestnuts/default.htm |archive-date=23 September 2011 }}</ref>
* Guignardia leaf blotch, caused by the fungus ''Guignardia aesculi''
* Wood rotting fungi such as ''[[Armillaria]]'' and ''[[Ganoderma]]''
* Horse chestnut scale, caused by the insect ''[[Pulvinaria regalis]]''
* Horse-chestnut leaf miner, ''[[Cameraria ohridella]]'', a leaf mining moth.<ref>{{cite web|title=Other common pest and disease problems of horse chestnut|url=http://www.forestresearch.gov.uk/website/forestresearch.nsf/ByUnique/INFD-6KYC5F| website= forestresearch.gov.uk| publisher=UK Forestry Commission|access-date=2010-01-09|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091209155131/http://www.forestresearch.gov.uk/website/forestresearch.nsf/ByUnique/INFD-6KYC5F|archive-date=2009-12-09}}</ref> The larvae of this moth species bore through the leaves of the horse chestnut, causing premature colour changes and leaf loss.<ref name= "suffolkcoastal" />
* Phytophthora bleeding canker, a fungal infection<ref>{{cite web |title=Bleeding Canker |url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/advicesearch/profile.aspx?PID=244 |date=11 November 2009 |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |access-date=2010-01-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100116184135/http://apps.rhs.org.uk/advicesearch/Profile.aspx?pid=244 |archive-date=16 January 2010 |url-status=live }}
</ref>

==Anne Frank tree==
{{Main|Anne Frank tree}}
A horse-chestnut tree stood outside the window of the [[Anne Frank House|"secret annex"]] in the centre of [[Amsterdam]], which [[Anne Frank]] mentioned in [[The Diary of a Young Girl|her diary]]; the tree survived until August 2010, when a heavy wind blew it over.<ref>{{cite news|title=Anne Frank's 'beautiful' tree felled by Amsterdam storm |first=Toby |last=Sterling|newspaper=The Scotsman |access-date=24 August 2010 |date=24 August 2010 |url= http://news.scotsman.com/news/Anne-Frank39s-39beautiful39-tree-felled.6490345.jp}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Anne Frank tree falls over in heavy wind, rain |first=Aaron |last=Gray-Block |newspaper=Reuters.com |access-date=24 August 2010 |date=23 August 2010 |url= https://www.reuters.com/article/idUSLDE67M1DH |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100824073648/https://www.reuters.com/article/idUSLDE67M1DH |archive-date= 24 August 2010 |url-status=live }}</ref> Eleven young specimens, sprouted from seeds from this tree, were transported to the United States. After a long quarantine in Indianapolis, each tree was shipped off to a new home at a notable museum or institution in the US, such as [[Liberty Park|9/11 Memorial Park]], [[Little Rock Central High School]], and two [[Holocaust]] Centers. One of them was planted outdoors in March 2013 in front of [[The Children's Museum of Indianapolis]], where they were originally quarantined.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.yahoo.com/news/saplings-anne-franks-tree-root-us-163048542.html|title=Saplings from Anne Frank's tree take root in US| website= yahoo.com| first= Pamela| last= Engel|date=24 March 2013|access-date=26 July 2018}}</ref>

==Symbol of Kyiv==
The horse chestnut tree is one of the symbols of [[Kyiv]], the capital of [[Ukraine]].<ref name="7253616chestnutKyivC">{{cite news| url= https://www.pravda.com.ua/articles/2020/05/29/7253616/ |title= 'Туйовий Хрещатик' Чому кияни сумують за каштанами та як вони стали символом столиці| first1= Євген| last1= Руденко| first2= Ельдар| last2= Сарахман| trans-title='Thujoy Khreshchatyk': Why Kyivans miss chestnuts and how they became a symbol of the capital| work= [[Ukrayinska Pravda]] |date= 29 May 2020| language= uk| access-date= 2025-09-30}}</ref>
